title: How Leaders Destroy Their Best Teams
author: The Best Leadership Newsletter
summary: The Best Leadership Newsletter argues that the single biggest predictor of high-performing teams is not individual talent, accountability, structure, hierarchy, or friendship — it is psychological safety. Drawing on Google's 2012 Project Aristotle research, the piece names the surprise finding: teams perform better when people feel safe to make mistakes, challenge ideas, and disagree without fear, and that particular condition outweighs every other variable leaders typically obsess over. The reason most leaders ignore this is ego: psychological safety can't be controlled or fixed by reorgs and processes, only created or destroyed by leader behaviour, which forces leaders to recognize that team performance problems are about them too. The piece walks through a real $30M-revenue tech-company case where a polished-on-paper leadership team agreed too quickly, hard conversations were pushed aside, and silence was misread as alignment by the CEO; one diagnostic question ('what is one thing everyone here sees but no one feels safe to talk about?') and the silence that followed told the whole story. The author is explicit that psychological safety is not niceness or lowered standards — high standards are required for it, and the safest teams are the ones that argue and debate without fear of retaliation. Behaviours that destroy it: defensiveness toward feedback, emotional reaction to bad news, shutting down new ideas, subtle or overt berating for mistakes.
points: Google's Project Aristotle (2012) found psychological safety — whether people feel safe speaking up — was the number-one predictor of team effectiveness, beating talent, structure, management style, and IQ/EQ measures.

Leaders ignore psychological safety not because they doubt it but because it makes them feel less in control; it can't be measured on a dashboard or fixed by a reorg, only created or destroyed by leader behaviour.

Silence is not agreement: when no one pushes back, when meetings dodge tension, when decisions are too unanimous, that is usually missing safety, not real alignment — and the predictable consequences are hidden mistakes, dead innovation, slowing growth.
Psychological safety is not niceness or lowered standards; high standards are required for it. The safest teams argue and debate without fear of retaliation, which is what makes them safe.

What destroys safety in practice: defensiveness toward feedback, emotional reaction to bad news, shutting people down for new ideas, overt or subtle berating for mistakes — the leader's behaviour, not the policy, is what does it.
quotes: When it comes to creating a high-performing team, there's one trait that matters more than any other. It's not individual talent. It's not accountability. It's also not structure or hierarchy or even the team members being friends. The single most important element to successfully creating a high-performing team is… Psychological safety.

The number one predictor of successful teams is whether or not people feel safe speaking up. Teams perform better when people feel safe to make mistakes, challenge ideas, and disagree without fear. That's psychological safety.
Leaders don't ignore psychological safety because they think it doesn't matter. They ignore it because it makes them feel less in control. When it comes right down to it, control is about ego.
Psychological safety is created or destroyed by the leaders behavior. Period. Full stop. If you're the leader, you are fully responsible for psychological safety.

When no one pushes back on your ideas… When meetings don't address the tension… When most decisions seem to be unanimous… Some leaders call that alignment. But they're wrong. When there is no pushback, there is usually no psychological safety.

Maintaining high standards is really important for maintaining psychological safety. After all you can't have a high-performing team without high standards. The safest teams are the ones that argue and debate and disagree, and they can do it all without fear of retaliation or being berated.
You don't destroy psychological safety with your policies. You destroy it with your behavior.” Archived from The Best Leadership Newsletter on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
